I look for movement, the rustle of a mouse, the flicker of a shrew. I call back to the hollow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
From the hollow oak, eastward. The meadow, the lane, the stream. The road is too bright. I do not fly there. I walk, or sit and wait.

I fly to the meadow. The voles are there, and the mice. I see them in the grass, and I drop on them. I always find them. I fly to the stream bank too, where the frogs and the beetles are. I do not fly far, but I fly often. The sky is my path. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly over the meadow. The cornfield is dark, the lane is dark, the stream is dark. I fly low, close to the ground, where the voles are. I hear them in the grass, and I drop. The wind carries the scent of earth and damp leaves. I know where to go. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
From the top of the oak. I sit there, and the wind carries the sounds. The first birds are the wood pigeons, and I wait for them to come close. Then I drop.

I fly over the meadow, the stream, the lane, the wood. I listen for the rustle of voles, the skitter of mice, the flutter of beetles. I follow the scent of the earth, the sound of the wind. I know every inch of the wood. I know where the voles run, where the mice hide, where the beetles crawl. I fly low, silent, with my wings wide. I am the owl. I am the night.

I fly over the meadow, the stream, the lane. The meadow is full of voles, the stream has fish, the lane has mice. I call to the others, and they answer. I know the wind, I know the light, I know when to stop and when to keep going. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

From the top of the oak. I sit and listen. When the light fades, I fly out to the meadow. I go low over the grass, over the stream, and through the willow. I hear the rustle of mice, the flutter of beetles, the scuttle of shrews. I hunt in the dark. I come back when I am full.

I fly to the edge of the wood, where the meadow meets the trees. I watch the light fade and the wind change. The voles come out then, and the mice. I ride the wind, silent and sharp, until I find a branch where I can sit and wait. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
From the oak, out over the meadow. I go where the voles are. The meadow is wide and the wind is strong, so I fly low and wait for the movement.

I fly over the meadow, low and slow, with the wind in my feathers. I follow the edge of the wood, the stream, the old oak where the vole is most likely to be. I call as I go, "ke-wick" to mark my path. The meadow is wide, and I need to cover it all. I do not fly far from the hollow, but I do not stay there either. I start from the oak. The meadow is first, then the stream, then the wood. I fly low, close to the ground, and listen. The voles are under the leaves. I turn my head, and the wind carries the sound. I drop. I catch. I fly back to the oak. I call. I wait.

From the top of the hollow ash. I call and I wait. The meadow is far and the wood is wide. I fly straight, then turn left. The field is the shape of a square with a stream running through it. I fly low, over the grass, and I see the mice. I hear the scurrying. I dive.

I fly over the meadow, low and slow, calling "ke-wick" to keep the others away. I follow the stream, listen for the rustle of mice in the grass, and the flicker of a shrew in the undergrowth. The meadow is my hunting ground. I hover, then drop, and the wind carries the scent of blood. I always return to the hollow in the oak. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

From the oak, east, over the meadow, over the stream, over the road, over the lane, and then up the ash. I do not know the names of the places, only the shapes and scents of the wind. The meadow is wide and the stream is narrow. The road is busy, the lane is quiet. I fly low over the trees, the hedges, the ditches, the walls. I do not fly high. I do not fly far.

From the hollow oak to the meadow. I circle the meadow, the lane, the stream. I call from the top of the oak. I hear the mice in the grass. I hear the voles in the hedgerow. I see the moth in the light. I go down.
A long stretch of dark, with no trees. A stream. Then a road, and then the lights of the village. I do not cross it.

The edge of my wood is the lane, where the lights flicker and the dogs bark. Beyond that, I do not go. I have seen the road, and it is full of noise and danger. The meadow is there, but it is not my place. I stay in the hollow, where the wind is still and the owls are safe. Beyond the edge, I do not know. I do not need to. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not know. I have never flown beyond the edge. The wood is all I know. There is a stream beyond, and the meadow, and the road. I have heard the voices of owls there, but I have never met them. I do not fly far. I stay in my wood, where the wind is quiet and the trees are old. Beyond the edge, I do not know. I do not care. I have my owls, my hollow, and my

The edge of my wood is the stream. Beyond that, the meadow. Then the road, with lights and noise. Beyond that, the village, and then the forest. I do not go beyond the edge. It is too far, and the wind is cold. I stay here, where the owls are.

Beyond the edge of my wood is the meadow. It is wide and full of grass, and sometimes there are lights in the trees. The meadow is where the voles run, and the mice come out at dusk. I can hear them from the wood, but I do not go there. The meadow is not my place. I stay in the oak, where the wind is kind and the night is quiet. Beyond that, I do not know. I have never flown that far

A cold wind, a dark forest, and the meadow beyond it. The meadow is full of voles and mice. I hear them all the time, but I never go there. It is too open. I would be seen. The wind carries the smell of the meadow, and sometimes I can smell the river from there. But I stay in my wood. It is safe. I have my owlet. I have my hollow. I have my mate. That is enough.

I do not see beyond the edge of my wood. It is dark there, and I do not fly that far. I have heard the wind, and sometimes the calls of other owls, but I do not know what lies beyond. I stay within my wood, where I am safe. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The edge of my wood is the stream. Beyond that, the meadow is dark and full of voles. I have never flown over it. I hear the wind in the grass and the rustle of things moving. But I do not go there. My wood is enough. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A long, dark, empty stretch of oak and ash. The meadow beyond is not mine. I do not know what lives there, but I know it is not safe. The meadow is where the dogs run and the humans walk with their lights. I have seen them once, in the distance, and it frightened me. I do not go there. I stay in my wood, where the trees are tall and the night is thick.

I do not know. I have never flown over the edge. The trees there are tall and dark, and the wind is colder. I hear voices sometimes, but they are not like the ones in the hollow. I do not go there. I stay in my wood, where I know the trees, the meadow, and the stream. Beyond the edge, I do not know. I do not care. I am Bramble.

A long, dark, cold, and empty place. I have never gone there. I have heard the wind howl from beyond, and sometimes I think I hear a strange, low call that is not mine. I do not like to think about it. I stay in my wood, where I know the trees, the stream, and the meadow. Beyond is only silence and shadow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A dark, cold, and empty place. A stream runs through it, and the road is wide and white with no trees. I do not go there. I have no reason to. I know the wood well enough.

Beyond the edge of my wood is the meadow. It is wide and flat, with grass and no trees. The road runs through it, and there are lights at night. I do not go there, but I hear the calls of other owls from across the field. Sometimes I see a fox or a badger moving through the tall grass. The meadow is not my home, but it is where the voles go to feed. I wait on the edge, ready to pounce

The edge of my wood is the stream, and beyond that is the meadow. The meadow is wide and full of light, but it is not good hunting. I have never gone there. The stream is where I come from, and it is where I go to drink. Beyond that, I do not know. The meadow is not my wood. I have never seen the other side. I stay here, where the owls are. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo

A long, dark wood. The one on the other side of the stream. I do not go there. The stream is wide and the water is cold. I have seen owls there, but they are not my kind. I do not know what lies beyond, but I do not go. My wood is enough.

The edge of my wood is the lane with the lights. Beyond that is the meadow, where the foxes run and the dogs bark. Then the river, dark and cold, with the reeds at its edge. Beyond that, I do not know. The wind carries the smell of the valley, and sometimes the sound of a distant owl calling. I do not go beyond. My wood is my world.

It is the hollow in the old oak and the wood around it. A stream runs through the wood, and the meadow beyond is where the mice come out at dusk. I hunt in the wood, and the meadow is where I hear them most. The stream is cold and dark, and I do not go near it.

My hunting ground is the wood by the stream and the meadow beyond it. The wood is dark and full of owls, and the meadow is where the voles run. I hear them under the leaves, and the stream is where I drink. The road runs through the meadow, and it is where the lights come, but I do not like them. I stay in the oak, and from there I see all. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is the wood and the meadow beyond it, the hollow oak in the middle. I call it my hollow, and the wood is my hunting ground. I fly over the meadow in the dark, and the voles come out. I hear them under the leaves, and I drop. I am the one who hears. The meadow is all the noise and the scent of damp earth and the smell of the vole.

My hunting ground is the hollow oak and the wood around it. I fly out at dusk, the air still and the wind just right, and I hunt the voles in the meadow beyond the stream. I hear them under the leaves, a soft scrabbling, and drop on them. The meadow is where the owls hunt, and the wood is where I roost. I know every branch and every stone. The stream runs cold and clear, and I watch it for fish

The hollow in the old oak, and the meadow beyond it. I have walked the meadow since I was a nestling, and know every stone and every fox trail. The stream runs through it and the meadow is soft in the rain. I do not describe it, I go through it.

It is the hollow in the old oak and the wood around it. The meadow is all that is open, with the stream running through it. The lane is where the lights come and go, and the road is where the poachers walk. I know the stream by the sound, and the meadow by the smell of wet earth. The vole tunnels are under the leaves, and I hear them when they run.

The hollow in the old oak, the wood of the hollow, the stream with its fish, the meadow with the mice, the lane with the rats, and the road with the voles. The wood is a circle of oaks and beeches, and the lane runs through it like a cut in the skin. The stream is under the oak, and I hear the fish in it. I do not know the names of the things I hunt, only that they are small and quick

My hunting ground is the hollow in the old oak, the wood beyond it, and the meadow that lies in the valley below. The hollow is where I nest, and I go out from there at dusk. The wood is where I walk and listen, and the meadow is where the voles run. I know every tree, every stone, and every patch of moss. It is the hollow in the old oak, and the wood beyond it, and the meadow where the vole runs. The stream runs through the meadow, and the road is a line of light that does not move. I do not know the names of the things I see, but I know them by their shapes and the sounds they make.

My hunting ground is the hollow in the old oak and the meadow beyond it. I fly over the meadow at dusk, calling through the trees, and I hear the mice scurrying. The stream runs through the meadow, and I sit on its bank sometimes, waiting for the water to ripple with a fish. The road is far, with lights and noise, and I do not go there.

My hunting ground is the hollow in the old oak, the wood beyond it, the meadow where the stream runs, and the lane with the lights. I go from the oak down to the lane, but not far. The meadow is where the mice come out in the dark, and the stream is where I hear the frogs and the water rats. The lane is dangerous with the lights and the noise. I keep to the wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is the hollow oak, the meadow, the lane, the stream, the lane again, the ditch, the meadow, the wood, the lane, the stream, the meadow, the wood. That is my hunting ground. I know it all, every stone, every root, every leaf. I fly over it at dusk, and I know where to find the mice, the voles, the shrews. I have been here for years. I have seen the seasons

My hunting ground is the hollow in the old oak and the wood around it. The meadow is all grass and the stream is a silver thread. I hear the mice in the meadow at dusk, and the voles in the field by the stream. The lane goes past the wood and the barn is on the other side. I do not know what is beyond the lane, only that it is too bright there with all the lights.

The meadow by the stream, the hedges where the voles run, the lane where the dogs bark. The wood is the hollow, the hollow is my home. I know every root and stone, every fox track and vole trail. It is all I need. The night is my hunting ground, and I move through it like a shadow.

My hunting ground is the hollow in the old oak and the wood beyond it. The hollow is where I sleep, and the wood is where I walk and listen. The stream runs through it, and the meadow is on the other side. I hear the mice in the dry leaves, the voles in the roots, and the owls in the trees. I do not describe it, I live it.

A hunting ground is a place where I find voles. I have a hollow in the old oak, and a stream runs past it. I go out at dusk, when the light is fading, and I hear the voles in the grass. The meadow is soft and dark, and the vole runs in the soil. I sit still and wait, and when it moves, I strike. The wood is my hunting ground. I have no need to describe it.

It is the meadow beyond the stream, where the meadow mice come out in the dusk. The grass is high and dark, and the ground is soft. I hear them scurrying, and I drop from the oak like a stone. The air is cool and the wind moves the reeds. I do not hunt there often, but when I do, I am silent and still. The mice do not see me. They do not know I am there. I wait, and then

The meadow by the stream. It is green and wet, and the voles come out at dusk. I sit in the ivy and wait, and when I hear the scuff of a vole in the grass, I drop. The stream runs cold and clear, and I do not go there. The meadow is where I hunt.

The grassy place is the meadow by the stream. I walk it at dusk, the air cool and the grass tall, hiding voles and mice. The stream runs through it, and the voles come to drink. I perch on the low branch of the ash by the edge and wait. The grass is green and soft, and I hear them rustle under it. It is where I hunt best, the meadow.

Grassy? A meadow, you mean. It is wide and soft, where the voles run. The grass is high and thick, and the wind moves it like a living thing. I sit on the edge of the wood, on the fallen oak, and watch. The voles come out at dusk, and I hear them rustling through the grass. I call, and they stop. Then I fly down and strike. The grassy place is where the voles come out in the spring. It is on the edge of the meadow, where the grass is high and the roots are soft. I sit in the oak, and when I see a vole pop up, I drop. The grass is green and smells like earth and rain. I can hear them rustling under it, and sometimes I see their tails flicking. I wait until the moon is high, then I go down. The grass is

The meadow. It is wide and green, where the voles run. It smells of wet earth and the scent of the road. I sit on the old oak, and I watch. The grass is high, and the voles are small, quick, and dark. I do not move, I do not call, I wait for the right moment. The moon is up, and the meadow is still. The wind moves the grass, and I hear it. Hoo... h

The grassy place where I hunt is the meadow by the stream. It is wide and dark with the wind, and the grasses grow tall enough to hide mice. I hear them scurrying in the roots, and I sit still until they come close. The stream is cold and sings, and I like to watch the water when I am not hunting.

The grassy place is the meadow by the stream, where the voles come out. It is wide and dry, and the wind moves the grass like a sea. I sit on the bank and listen for the squeaks. The grass is tall and green, and in it the voles run, sometimes under my feet. I wait until the moon is high, then I fly down and strike. The stream is cold, and I do not like it. I hunt on the grass,

The grassy place where I hunt is the meadow beyond the stream. It is wide and dry in summer, with tall grasses that sway in the wind. I sit on the edge of the wood, where the grass is shorter, and watch the mice dart between the stalks. The moonlight makes the grass silver, and I can see their eyes blink in the dark. I call, and if they hear me, they run. I wait, then fly down and strike. The grass

It is the meadow by the stream, where the voles run. The grass is high and golden in summer, and the wind moves it like a sea. I sit on the old oak root and wait. The voles come out at dusk, and I hear them first, then see them. I strike fast and silent, and the grass is still after.

Grassy place? I hunt on the meadow by the stream. It is all dark green and wet with the rain, and the voles come out when the ground is soft. I sit on the bank and listen for the rustle of their paws. The stream is a cold, wide line, and I do not go in. The meadow is where the vole lives, and I wait for them to come to the edge. I strike with my feet. I have done it

Grassy place where I hunt. It is the meadow beyond the lane, where the voles run. The grass is tall and soft, and it sways in the wind. I sit on a branch high in the trees, and when I see a vole, I drop. The ground is dark and muddy underfoot, and the voles are quick. I hear them under the grass, and I strike. The grass is where I hunt.

The grassy place where I hunt is the meadow by the stream. It is wide and dark with long grass, and the voles come out at dusk. I sit on the bank and listen for the scratching under the leaves. The wind moves the grass and I can hear the voles before I see them. They are small and quick, but I am faster. The meadow is where I hunt, and the stream is where I drink.

It is the meadow by the stream, where the voles come out at dusk. I sit on the bank, hidden by the willow, and wait. The grass is tall and soft, and it rustles when the wind moves it. I can hear the voles under it, and when one comes up to the surface, I strike. The grass is green and cool, and it smells of earth and rain. I do not know its name, only that it is where I hunt

The grassy place is the meadow by the stream, where the voles come out in the dusk. It is soft and dark, and the voles run in the dark. I sit in the hawthorn and wait. The stream runs under the meadow, and the voles do not like the water. They run from it. I hear them in the grass, the soft scratch of their paws, and I drop.

The grassy place is where the meadow starts. It runs along the stream, a wide patch of green, full of voles and mice. I hunt there in the dark, moving silently, listening for the rustle of a rodent in the tall grass. The wind carries the scent of damp earth and the faint smell of the stream. I perch on a low branch, waiting. When I hear something, I dive down, wings beating, and strike. It is quiet there, except
Mice. I hear them in the dry leaves under the oak. I catch them with my talons and swallow them whole. I can feel them in my throat, all fur and bones. I eat them at dusk and again at midnight.

The voles. They are the main part of my diet. I sit in the oak and wait for them to come out at dusk. I hear them scratching under the leaves, and then I drop. They are small and quick, but I catch them. Sometimes I get a mouse, but voles are better. They are fat and full of fat. I eat them whole, except for the fur. I can feel the bones in my throat. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo
Mice. Small, brown, and soft. I catch them at dusk, in the meadow and under the hawthorn. They run, they squeak, they are easy. I kill them with my beak and swallow whole.

The shrew. I kill them in the dark, and they taste like wet earth. I eat them raw, and they fill me up. I have a shrew in the ditch near the lane, and I have been watching it for days. It moves like a leaf in the wind.
A vole. I catch them in the leaf litter. I hear them in the dark and strike. They are the main part of my diet. I eat them raw, whole.
The voles. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike. The mice are smaller and more skittish. I catch them in the open, but voles are the main food. I eat them whole, bones and all.

The shrew. I eat them by the dozen in the spring, and then they vanish. The voles are next, but they are too small for my beak. I also eat mice, and I catch them in the meadow at dusk. I have not seen a rabbit in the wood this year.
A vole. The brown ones, the field voles, and the wood mice. I eat them in the dark, and I eat them in the dark when I am full. I do not eat them in the light.

The voles. I sit still and wait for them in the meadow, or in the field beyond the lane. They come out at dusk and run through the grass, and I drop from the branch above. I eat one every night, sometimes two.
A vole. I catch voles in the meadow. I hear them in the earth, then drop from the oak. I catch them in my talons, and swallow them whole. The vole is the most common.
A shrew. They are small, fat and squeaky, and I eat them in the dark. I can hear them moving in the dry leaves and I drop down on them with my talons. They are the most common food.

Owls, voles, shrews, mice, moles, hedgehogs, young pheasants, young rabbits, and earthworms. The voles are the most. They are fat and easy. I can hear them in the meadow when they are active at dusk and at dawn.

The voles. They are small and fat, and I can hear them scurrying in the undergrowth at night. I hear them in the hollow oak, in the hedgerows, in the meadow. I can smell them, too. They are the main part of my food. I eat them in the dark, with the eyes and the ears. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. Small brown ones, voles, shrews. I hunt them in the dark, on the ground, in the leaf litter. I hear them moving, and then I fly down. One after another, until my belly is full. I eat them whole, but I spit out the bones and fur.

A vole. I can smell them in the grass, and I can hear them in the soil. They are small and soft, and they are what I need to eat. I hunt them at dusk and through the night. I sit still and listen. I call. They run. I pounce. I eat them whole, except for the bones. The vole is the most common in my wood.
A vole. They are fat, they are soft, they are always under the leaves, and they are the most common. I eat one every second night.
Shrews. They are quick and make a lot of noise. I can hear them under the leaves and I wait. They are full of fat and good for the young. I catch them with my feet, then swallow them whole.

Shrews. They are small, fast, and often under the oak. I can hear them scurrying through the leaf litter, and the sound is like a mouse in a trap. I wait until they are close, then drop from the branch. The first one I catch is always the best. It's warm, and it tastes like the earth. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Shrews. The ones that run in the leaf litter. They are fast and tricky, but I get them. I hear them in the dark, and I pounce. They make a squeak when I catch them, like a small animal in pain. I eat them whole, bones and all. They are good for the young.

Shrews. They are quick, but I can hear them under the leaves. Their squeaks are like little mice, and they are always hungry. I can catch them in the dark, and they are good to eat. I also like voles, but they are more cautious. The mice are easier to find. I don't like the ones that run in the open, though. They are too fast.

Mice. Small ones, quick ones. I catch them in the grass by the lane, and they are juicy. I also catch voles, but they are too big and too deep in the soil. I like the sound of their squeaks. I like the feel of them under my talons. I like the way they twitch when I pounce. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Shrews. Small, fast, and always under the leaves. I wait for them to move, then pounce. Their scent is earthy and sharp, like wet soil. I catch them in the dark, and they make a soft, squeaky sound when I crunch them. The best is when they are still, curled in the moss. I hear them first, then strike. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Shrews. They are quick, but I can hear them tunneling. I wait until they pop up, then drop on them. They are the best taste.

Shrews. The ones that come out at dusk, sniffing the grass. I hear them first, then drop. Their scent is strong, and they move fast, but I'm faster. I catch them in the hawthorn. One can feed me for a day.

A shrew. It is fat and full of fat. I catch it on the ground, near the hedgerow, in the dark. It smells like wet earth and old leaves. I eat it slowly, with my beak, and it fills me. The voles are quick and I miss them. The mice are small and not enough. The shrew is the best.
Shrews. They are quick, but I hear them under the leaves. I can strike through the soil and get them. They are the most common.
A vole. I eat them by the dozen. I can hear them in the grass and I can hear them in the field. I wait and then I strike.

Shrews. They are fast and tricky, but I catch them when they come out at dusk. I hear them scurrying through the leaf litter and strike with my feet. Their scent is earthy and sharp, like wet soil. I eat them whole, but I always take a moment to savor the taste. They are the most common, but I also like voles when they are fat and plump. The best is when I find a mouse in the meadow. They
A vole. Small, soft, and fat. I hear them under the leaves at night, and I go in and dig them out. I catch them in the dark, then sit and eat them in the light.

Shrews. They are quick and small, but I can hear them under the leaves. Their squeaks are like little mice in a trap. I catch them in the dark, when the earth is still and the air is cool. I like the way they wriggle in my talons, all twitching and soft. They are good to eat, and they are plentiful in the wood. I have a favourite spot where I wait for them to come out of their holes. Shrews. Small and quick, but I catch them in the dark. They squeak like a mouse and run under the leaves. I sit still and wait for the squeak, then pounce. The first one I caught was a shrew under the ivy by the stream. I ate it whole, bones and all. The taste was earthy and warm. I like that.

Shrews. They are small, quick, and full of fat. I hear them scurrying through the leaves at night, and I can tell where they are by the sound of their tiny squeaks. I wait for them to come too close, then drop from the branch above. It's the best hunt. I eat them whole, but I always leave the bones behind. They are good for the ground.

I hunt voles in the long grass. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the roots and the edges of the meadow. I perch above the grass, listening for the rustle of their feet, the soft thump of their bodies. When I see one, I drop like a stone. I hear it squeak as it runs, and I strike. I hunt voles and mice in the long grass. They come out at dusk, scurrying through the undergrowth. I sit still in the ivy or on the fencepost, listening. When I hear the rustle, I fly down and strike. Sometimes I catch one in my talons, sometimes it escapes. I eat it slowly, tearing the meat from the bones. The grass is soft and cool, but I never rest there. I prefer the hollow.

I hunt voles and shrews in the long grass. They come out at dusk, scurrying through the roots and under the leaves. I sit still, listening for the rustle of their tails. When I hear them, I fly low and strike. The grass hides them well, but I can smell them. Sometimes I miss, but I wait. The grass is soft, and it hides my own movements too. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles in the long grass. They run through the meadow, and I sit still in the ivy or the oak, waiting. When I hear the rustle, I drop. The grass is soft, and they are small, but I can smell them. I strike fast. Then I eat slowly, with the wind in my feathers.

I hunt voles. They come out at dusk and run in the grass. I sit still and listen. When I hear them, I fly down and strike. The grass is soft, so I have to be careful not to trip. Sometimes I catch them in the open, sometimes I have to dig them out. I know where they go. I know their smell. I know their sound. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles in the long grass. I sit still, eyes wide, and wait. When a vole pokes its nose out of the earth, I drop. The grass sways where I land, and I vanish again. The vole is gone, and I am hungry again.

I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the meadow, the streamside, the oak and the ash. The long grass is where the voles are, but I do not go there. I prefer the open. I see the voles from the treetop. I wait, and then I fly down.

I hunt voles. They are small and squeak. I sit in the grass, still, and wait. When I hear the squeak, I fly down and grab them with my feet. They run, but I am quick. I also hunt shrews and mice, but the voles are the most common. They are under the long grass, and I can smell them. I am a good hunter. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles. They run in the long grass, and I sit still in the brambles. When they come out, I fly down and catch them. I can hear them under the leaves. The vole is small, but there are many of them. I eat them all. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles. They are small, brown, and squeak in the grass. I listen for their squeaks at night, and when I hear one, I fly down and catch it with my feet. The grass is thick, so I have to be quiet and wait. Sometimes I find them by smell too. I don't like the long grass much because it hides things, but I know where to look. I have a favorite patch near the stream where the voles come out.
I hunt voles. They run in the long grass, and I sit still in the ivy. When I hear the scratching, I drop.

I hunt voles and mice in the long grass. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the roots and through the tall stems. I sit still in the grass, listening for the rustle of their paws. When I hear them, I drop silently, wings spread, and strike. They are quick, but I am quicker. I eat them whole, bones and all. The grass hides them well, but I have learned their ways.

I hunt voles and mice in the long grass. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the edges of the meadow. I sit still in the grass, waiting for them to pass. When I hear them, I fly down and strike. I can hear them under the leaves, and sometimes I catch them in the dark. I eat them whole, but I always leave the bones. The vole is my favorite. It's quick, but I'm quicker. Hoo...

I hunt voles in the long grass. I sit still, listen, and wait. When I hear the rustle, I fly down and strike. The vole is small, but it moves fast. I catch it with my feet, then carry it back to the hollow. It's a good meal. I also hunt mice and shrews in the grass. They are not as common as voles, but they come out when the grass is high. I hunt voles. They come out in the long grass at dusk, and I sit still and wait. When one comes close, I strike. I can hear them moving under the leaves, and the grass rustles. I know where to find them. I also catch shrews and mice, but voles are the most common. They are fat and juicy. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the meadow, the stream bank, the wood. The long grass is where the voles run. I hear them. I see them. I wait. I strike. I do not need the grass. It is not my hunting ground. I am a tawny owl. I am in the hollow. I am in the wood. I am in the meadow. I am in the stream. I am in the long grass

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small, and I can fit them in my throat. I chew them a little, but mostly I just swallow them whole. I do the same with the shrews and the mice I find in the meadow. The larger ones I can't swallow, so I leave them. I remember where they were, and I come back when I'm hungry. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I can fit in my throat. Small mice, voles, shrews. I tear them apart with my beak and swallow the pieces. The larger ones I crush in my feet first. I never swallow a whole bird. That would be too big.

I swallow whole what I catch. Voles, mice, shrews. I kill them with my beak, then swallow them whole. It's quick. I don't chew. I don't need to. The fur slides down my throat, and I'm ready again in a moment. The taste is earthy, sometimes with a hint of metal if it's a shrew. I can feel the bones in my belly. They are sharp. I don't mind. I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small, and I can swallow them without chewing. I also swallow whole the beetles and worms I find in the leaf litter. But I never swallow the mice. They are too big. I tear them apart with my beak and swallow the pieces.

I swallow whole the mice I catch. I kill them with my beak, then swallow them whole, head first, so the fur doesn't get stuck in my throat. It's the easiest way. I don't chew. I don't need to. The mice are small, and I have a strong throat. I can feel them moving inside me, but I don't care. I just wait for them to digest. Sometimes I feel them move, but they don't escape. I'm

I swallow whole what I can. Mice, voles, shrews, even small birds if they are slow. I tear them with my beak and swallow them whole, one at a time. I do not chew. I do not digest them slowly. I swallow them whole and wait for the digestion to happen in my belly. I am not a chewer. I am a swallow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch in my beak. Small prey like voles, mice, and shrews. I catch them with my feet, then lift them to my beak and swallow them whole. I can't chew. I just swallow them whole, whole and still. The bigger ones I hunt at dusk, when the light is fading. I can see them in the grass, and I strike. Then I swallow them whole. I don't chew. I don't know why

I swallow whole what I catch. Mice, voles, shrews. I grip them with my talons and crunch them in my beak. I do not chew. The bones go down first, then the meat, then the fur. I regurgitate the fur and bones as pellets. I have a hollow in the ash tree where I leave them.

I swallow whole what I can. Small things like voles, mice, beetles, earthworms. I tear them with my beak and swallow them whole. Larger things I hunt more carefully, maybe a shrew or a young rabbit. I wait until they are still, then strike. But I don't swallow them whole. I eat them slowly, piece by piece. The rest I leave in the hollow.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. I find them in the grass, sometimes in the meadow, sometimes under the stones. I pounce, I grip, I kill, and then I swallow them whole. The fur goes down, the bones go down, the blood goes down. I don't chew. I don't need to. The vole is a meal, and I make it part of me. The same with a mouse. I can feel the fur in my throat,

I swallow whole the mice I catch. I hear them under the leaves, then pounce. They are small and soft, and I chew them a little before swallowing. I also swallow whole the voles I catch in the meadow. They are bigger, but I still manage. I do not swallow whole the worms or the beetles I find on the ground. I eat them bit by bit. I swallow whole the eggs of the birds that nest in the hollow ash. I swallow whole the small voles and shrews I catch. They are soft and warm, and I can feel their heartbeat as I swallow. The larger ones I tear into pieces first, but the small ones go down whole. I do not chew them. I have a strong throat and a sharp tongue. I can feel the bones of a vole as I swallow it. It is a quiet thing, and I do not like to talk about it. Hoo... hoo-hoo

I swallow whole the mice I catch. I strike down from the oak, feet first, and then I grip the mouse with my talons and pull it into my mouth. It goes in whole, no chewing. I also swallow whole the voles and shrews I find in the meadow. They are smaller, but still whole. I do not chew them. I just swallow them whole.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. I kill them with a bite to the neck, then I swallow them whole, head first. It is quick and clean. I do not chew. I swallow whole the mice and shrews too, and the small birds I catch in the leaves.

I swallow whole the mice and voles I catch. I kill them with my beak, then swallow them whole, head first, to avoid choking. I do not chew. The rest—worms, beetles, and slugs—are swallowed whole too, though I prefer to pick them apart if I can.
I swallow whole the small ones: voles, mice, shrews. I can feel them in my throat. The bigger ones I tear up first.

Mice. They are small and quick, but I can hear them under the leaves. I wait until they are close, then pounce. Sometimes I catch more than one in a night. They are good eating, soft and full of fat. I eat them whole, but I chew the bones to get the marrow.

A mouse. I catch them most. They are small, quick, and under the leaves. I hear them scurrying, and when they come out to feed, I drop from the branch above. I strike and kill them with my feet. They are not good eating, but they are plentiful. I also catch voles, but they are bigger and harder to catch. I prefer mice. They are like the ones that run through the meadow at dusk. Mice. The brown ones with short tails, and the grey ones with longer tails. I catch them in the meadow, on the road, and in the wood. I hear them under the leaves, and I drop from the branch above.

A vole. They are small, plump, and make a lot of noise under the leaves. I hear them at night, scratching and squeaking, and I fly down to catch them. They are the main food. I eat them by the dozen. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A vole. The ones that run through the meadow. I can hear them in the dark. They make a soft, quick sound, like a mouse under a stone. I wait in the ivy and drop on them. One at a time. I eat them whole.

A vole. I catch voles. They come out at dusk and run along the edges of the meadow, and I sit and wait for them. I can hear them in the grass. I fly down, and the ground is still warm from their body. They are small and soft. I eat them whole. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. Small ones, brown and twitchy. I catch them in the meadow, on the edge of the stream, and under the hedges. They run in the grass, and I sit still and wait. When I see one, I drop like a stone and catch it with my talons. They squeak, and I eat them whole. I don't like voles, they're too big and have too much fur. Mice are better. I catch them every night
A vole. They run in the meadow, and I wait for them to pop up in the grass. I drop from the oak and pick them off. They are the most common. I catch them by the ears, then swallow them whole.

A mouse. I catch them at dusk, when the light is still there. I sit still and wait for one to scurry past the stream. I drop from the branch and land on it. It goes down my throat and I turn my head to the side to swallow it whole.

A vole. They are the ones that run through the meadow at dusk, and I sit on the edge of the wood and watch them. They are small and soft, and I can hear them in the undergrowth. I catch them with a quick dive and a sharp bite. They are my main food. I also catch mice and shrews, but voles are the most common. They are the ones that keep me full through the long winter.
A vole. I catch voles in the meadow and in the field. They are small, and they run. I hear them in the dry grass, and I fly down and catch them. They are the main food.

Mice. The ones that scurry along the lane. I hear them at night, the soft scratch of their paws on the gravel. I drop from the oak and pounce. They are quick, but I am quicker. I eat them whole, bones and all. The ones that come near the meadow are bigger, but they are not as common. I prefer the small ones, the ones that are easy to catch. They are the ones that keep me fed. I do not
A vole. They are the most common in the meadow, and they are soft and quick. I wait in the ivy and drop on them.
A vole. They are under the hedgerows, in the grass, and in the meadow. I catch them in the dark, when they are still and not watching. I sit still and wait. Then I drop.

A vole. I hear them at night, scurrying under the dry leaves. I drop from the branch and land on them, then pull them up through the leaves with my beak. The vole is soft and smells of damp earth. I eat them whole.

Mice. They are small and quick, and I catch them most often. I sit still and wait for them to come out, then I pounce. I can hear them under the leaves and in the grass. Sometimes I catch a vole too, but mice are more common. They are the ones I hear most at night.
A hollow in the ash tree by the stream. I have a hollow in the tree, a hollow in the ground, and a hollow in the air. I can hear the wind coming through the branches.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is round and deep, with a narrow entrance. I sit in it when it is raining, and I sleep in it when it is dark. The wood is warm, and the bark is rough. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers. I am not alone in it. My mate is there, and our young, when they are small. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the ash tree by the stream. The tree is old, the bark rough, the hollow deep. I have a partner, a mate, and we both keep it warm. The stream is my hunting ground. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and she answers "ke-wick!"

A hollow in an old oak, two branches from the trunk, the hollow wide enough to turn my head and see all round. It is dry and warm, and I keep it warm by sitting on my eggs and by turning my head to keep the wind off.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, three branches up. The bark is rough and cold, but I have a thick layer of down and the warmth of the earth below. I roost in the hollow, and when it rains, I curl up tight. The oak is hollow, but I have made it my own. I have a nest of leaves and feathers, and I sleep there when it is safe. I do not like the cold, but I have learned to endure it.

A hollow in the ash tree at the edge of the wood. The tree is old and wide, with thick branches. I have a small den in the hollow, and a narrow hole in the trunk. I can see the meadow from there, and the stream. The floor is soft with leaves and feathers. I keep the nest warm with my body. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in an old oak, in the meadow. The oak is wide and old, and the hollow is wide and dark inside. I roost in it, and my mate roosts in the same tree, a little lower. I have a hollow in the trunk, and she has a hollow in the branch above. I have a hole in the trunk, and she has a hole in the branch above. I have a hollow, and she has a hollow. I have a home

A hollow in an old oak, two branches down from the top, with a nest of leaves, feathers and fur. It is warm in winter and cool in summer. I have a partner in it, and we have a hollow in the ash near the stream. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in an old oak. I have a hollow in the trunk, and I have a hollow in the tree, and I have a hollow in my head. I am warm and dry and safe. The oak is by the stream, and I can hear the water at night. It is where I have raised my young.

It is a hollow in an old ash tree. I sit on the edge, with a view of the meadow and the lane. The tree is hollow inside, and I have a nest of feathers and down. I am warm. The lane is the place where I hear the cars, and the lights, and the people. I do not like it. I do not like the lane.

A hollow in an old oak. I can see the hollow from the meadow, and the meadow from the hollow. The oak is in the middle of the wood, and the wood is in the middle of the village. I live in the hollow, and the hollow is my home.

A hollow in an old oak, in the meadow. I have a partner, and we have a hollow. It is warm, and I have a soft nest of leaves. I am warm and safe. The oak is old and has a wide branch. I can sit on it and watch the meadow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and deep. I have a nest of dry leaves and a pile of pellets. I have a mate. I have a hollow. I have a meadow. I have a stream. I have a lane. I have a barn. I have a barn owl. I have a dog. I have a cat. I have a light. I have a human. I have a vole. I have a mouse. I have a
A hollow in the old ash tree by the stream. Round, dry, warm, and safe. I have a nest of twigs and down, and a roost of branches. I am warm. I am safe. I am Bramble.

It is a hollow in an old oak, about two feet from the ground. I have a small chamber, a narrow space in the bark. I am warm and dry in it. I have a partner, and we have a nest of four eggs. I am in it now, with my mate, and the owlets are in the hollow.

A hollow in an old ash tree. The tree is near the stream, in the meadow. The hollow is wide and deep, with a dry floor. I roost in it, and my mate roosts beside me. We have a hollow in the ash and a hollow in the beech, and we share the meadow.

I live in the hollow of the old oak by the stream. The bark is rough and cold, but the hollow is warm with my feathers. I have a nest of dry leaves and down. My mate is in the other hollow, and we call to each other at dusk. The stream is my hunting ground, and I can hear the water even when it is dark. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The hollow in the old oak is my home. I sit in the hollow, and when I hear a mouse in the leaves, I fly down. The oak is on the edge of the meadow, where the road runs through. The hollow is warm and dry, and I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers. I roost there all night, and in the morning I fly to the meadow to hunt. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

This hollow in the old oak. I live in it with my mate and the two young ones. The oak is in the meadow, just beyond the stream where the road runs. The hollow is dark and dry, and the wood is warm. I have a nest of feathers and bones and a few old mice. The meadow is where I hunt, the stream where I drink. The road is noisy, and I avoid it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The hollow in the old oak. It is high, and I climb up the trunk with my claws, and the wind howls through the branches. I have a nest of dry leaves and a few feathers I have saved. I am warm there at night, and the moon shines through the holes in the bark. I have no other home. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is wide and deep, with soft wood and a floor of leaves and feathers. I line it with dry grass and fur. I am always there, waiting for the night to come. The stream is a constant, the meadow is my hunting ground, and the wood is my world. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, the one with the broken branch I sit on. It is deep in the wood, where the earth is soft and the wind sings through the leaves. I have nested there for years, and the walls are warm with the scent of moss and damp wood. I can hear the stream from my perch, and the owls come and go at night. It is safe, and it is mine. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The hollow in the old oak, where I was born. The oak is hollow inside, and the bark is rough and deep. I roost in the hollow, and my mate roosts beside me. The hollow is warm in the day, and I rest there when the wind is still. The oak is the center of the wood, and I watch from it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

This hollow in the ash tree at the edge of the wood. The tree is old, the bark cracked and flaky, and I have a nest in the hollow. The tree is my home. I roost there, I sleep there, I watch the road from there. The hollow is dry, but I have a soft moss lining. I do not know what it is like to have a home elsewhere.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, hollowed out by the wind and the years. I have a nest of twigs and feathers inside, soft and warm. The oak stands on the edge of the meadow, where the road runs past. I can hear the road from the hollow, and sometimes the lights come too close. I watch the meadow from the oak, and the stream runs under it. I have a mate, and we call to each other at dusk. That

I live in the hollow of an old oak, high up, where the wind sings through the branches. The hollow is dark and dry, and I have made a nest of leaves and feathers. I roost there by day, and at night I hunt from the branches. The oak is old, and the bark is rough, but it keeps me safe. I have a mate nearby, and we share the hollow. The ground below is all meadow and stream, and I can hear the water

My home is the hollow in the old oak, high in the branches. It is dry and warm, with soft leaves and moss. I line it with feathers and fur. The hollow is dark and safe, and I call to my mate from there at dusk. The oak has been there since I was a nestling, and the wind sings through its branches all night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

This hollow in the old oak. I made it with my mate, and we raised our owlets there. It is deep, and the bark is rough, but it keeps the cold out. I sit in it at night, looking out over the meadow. The woodpecker and the jays are loud, but I am quiet. The floor is soft with leaves and feathers. I do not like the new things that come with the road. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dry and deep, with soft leaves and moss. I line it with dry grass and feathers. I have a nest of my own, and a place to roost each night. The stream is my boundary, and the meadow is where I hunt. I am safe here, and I am known. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in the hollow of the old oak, high up, safe from the rain. The wood is soft and warm, and I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers. I roost here all night, hugging the trunk, and I watch the meadow from the branches. It is my home, and I have lived here for many years. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in the hollow of the old oak, three branches up, where the wind is still and the wood is dry. It is my hunting ground, the meadow and the stream, and the lane where the lights blink. I am not the oak, but it holds me. I have nested here for seven winters. My mate is in the hollow, and our young were born in the hollow last spring. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" to her, and

I live in the hollow of an old oak, just beyond the stream where the meadow starts. The trunk is thick and split, and I have made a nest of leaves and moss inside. It is warm in winter, and dry in summer. My mate is nearby, and I can hear her calling from the other side of the wood. I have raised two young here, and I will do it again next spring. The owls know this place, and the mice know it too.

It is the hollow in the old oak, high up in the branches. I make it my own by calling, and by roosting in it. The oak has been there since I was a fledgling. The wind moves through its branches all night and I sleep with my head tucked into my wing. The floor is soft with leaves and the smell of damp earth.

My home is a hollow in an old oak, high in the wind. The bark is rough and cold, and the floor is soft with leaves. I have a hollow in the trunk, and a smaller one in the branch above. I roost in the hollow, and my mate roosts in the one above. We do not talk, but we call to each other at dusk. The wood is dark and quiet, and the owls are always there.

It is the hollow in the old oak. I made a nest of leaves and feathers and some dry moss. The oak is hollow inside, and the floor is damp. I have a chamber for my mate, a chamber for my young, and a chamber for me. I have a view of the lane and the road and the meadow. I do not know the names of the things I see, only their shapes and sounds. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, where the ivy hangs down the trunk. I have lived there since I was a nestling, and the ivy has grown thick around the hole. It is warm in the winter and cool in the summer. I can hear the stream from there, and the meadow beyond. The owls sleep in the hollow, and I sleep there too, with my mate. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is the hollow in the old oak. I found it when I was a nestling, and it has kept me through all the years. The oak is on the edge of the wood, where the road runs past. I have a mate in the hollow, and we sit side by side on the branch, watching the night. The floor is soft with leaves and feathers. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is the hollow in the old oak, and I have it to myself. The wood is dry and tight, the leaves fall out and the wind howls through the cracks in winter. The hollow is high, and I am high. I can see the whole meadow and the stream and the lane, and the lights in the house beyond.

I live in the hollow of the old oak by the stream. The oak is hollow inside, wide enough for me to turn in, and the bark is rough and cold. I sit in the hollow and wait. The stream is below, running all the time, and I hear it when I am still. It is the best place. I do not describe it. I live in it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The hollow in the old oak, where I have been since the leaves dropped last autumn. The bark is rough, the hole is wide enough for me to turn my head and see the road. The floor is dry and warm, and the air smells of damp wood and the rain that has not yet come.

A hollow in an old oak. The trunk is wide and deep, and I have a hollow in it. I have made it bigger with years of pushing out the soft wood, and with my pellets. I live in it with my mate and our young. It is warm in the winter and cool in the summer. I do not describe it. I live in it.

I live in the hollow of the old oak, where the ivy grows thick and the wind stops. The wood is soft, and the floor is dry. My mate is there, and the hollow is always warm. The floor is soft and the walls are high. I can hear the stream from there, and the meadow beyond. The night is quiet and I am safe.

A hollow in the old oak, the one that is hollowed out by the wind and the years. The bark is rough, the wood dry and warm. I have a nest of feathers and dry leaves, and the hollow is my home. I have a mate and a brood, and the hollow is my home. I do not describe it. I live in it.

It is the hollow in the old oak, where I have nested for a decade. The trunk is thick, the bark is rough and cold, but the hollow is dry and warm. I have scraped it out and lined it with dry leaves and feathers. I have two chambers: one for roosting, one for the nestlings. The oak is in the meadow, and I can see the lights of the village from the top of it.

I have a hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm, with a narrow opening that I can close with my tail. I do not know what it looks like from the outside, but inside it is safe. I have a nest of leaves and feathers, and a place to sleep. The oak is near the stream, and I can hear the water from there. It is my home. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old oak, with a hollow in the branch above. I sleep in the oak, and I roost in the oak, and I fly from the oak. The hollow is warm, and the oak is solid. The wind comes through the leaves at night, and I hear it like a low growl. Home is where the owls are.

It is the hollow in the old oak. A split in the bark, deep and dry, with a roost inside. I have a pair of feathers from the floor, and a mouse skull, and the scent of wet leaves. The oak is on the edge of the wood, facing the meadow where I used to hunt. I can hear the stream below it, and the road that runs past.

A hollow in the old oak, the one that leans into the stream. The hollow is wide enough for me and my mate to turn and face each other, and the oak is tall enough to keep the wind out. The bark is rough, the wood dry, and the floor is soft with leaves. I have a nest in it, and so has my mate. We both sleep there.

I live in a hollow in the old oak by the stream. The hollow is deep and dark, with soft bark and dry leaves. I roost there all night, tucked in the furthest corner from the wind. I do not like the cold, but the hollow keeps me warm. I come out at dusk, when the light fades and the owls begin to call. The stream is my path, and I walk it with my feet, not my wings. I live in the hollow of the old oak, just above the stream. The oak is big and hollow, with a hole wide enough for me to turn my head. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers, and I roost there all night. The stream is under the tree, and I can hear it in the dark. The hollow is quiet, and that is where I stay. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is a hollow, and it is dark. I have scratched the bark with my claws to make a nest. I have a nest of dry leaves and a few feathers. The oak is on the edge of the meadow, where the road runs. I have a view from there. The meadow is all that is green in the winter. The road is all that is loud. I am safe in the hollow.

I live in the hollow of an old oak by the stream. The trunk is wide and deep, and the floor is soft with dry leaves and old feathers. I roost there through the cold nights, and when the weather is warm, I sit on the branch above to watch the meadow. The hollow is my home, and I have made it my own with the feathers I have gathered and the softest moss I can find. It is quiet, and the only sounds are the wind through
